caption: A pole of Gamma, in log form
A floating-point argument evaluates directly to a high-precision decimal
At a pole of Gamma, compute-engine gives the real log-magnitude's divergence, PositiveInfinity, rather than treating GammaLn as complex-analytic
wolfram.note: Wolfram's GammaLn[-1] is ComplexInfinity, the complex-analytic reading of a pole of Gamma.

caption: Complex arguments; here the principal $\ln\Gamma(z)$ and Wolfram's $\mathrm{LogGamma}$ agree, as the imaginary part stays inside $(-\pi, \pi]$
A huge inexact argument, far past a double, from Stirling's series: $\ln\Gamma(10^{1000}) \approx 2.3016 \times 10^{1003}$
Threads over a list, and the integer points reduce to $\ln((n-1)!)$, matching Wolfram's LogGamma[5] = Log[24]
To 30 significant digits, the last one correctly rounded
Used to get $\ln(n!)$ for large n without overflowing float64: $\ln(10!) = \operatorname{GammaLn}(11)$
An exact positive integer now reduces too, matching Wolfram's LogGamma[5] = Log[24] ($\ln 24 = 3\ln 2 + \ln 3$, compute-engine's own factored form for $\ln$ of a composite)
The derivative of $\ln\Gamma$ is the digamma function. See [[Digamma]]
Off the positive axis GammaLn is the principal $\ln\Gamma(z)$: at $z = -3/2$, where $\Gamma > 0$, that is real. See [[LogGamma]] for the continuation
wolfram.note: Wolfram's $\mathrm{LogGamma}[-1.5] = 0.860047 - 6.28319\,i$: its analytic continuation sits $-2\pi i$ from the principal log here.
